comment: Regorafenib is category 1, but it is off the DLL3/PRAME axis the patient nominated and buys PFS with no OS signal on trials that let controls cross over. With efficacy_toxicity_weight at 0.85 and 'accepts high-risk high-reward' on the record, ranking a low-ceiling TKI first cedes the antigen-directed shot this case exists to evaluate. Keep it as the safety net if the workup closes every door, not as the headline.

target_intervention_label: DLL3 IHC (SP347) + PRAME IHC + HLA-A*02:01 typing
comment: No argument here: batching DLL3 IHC, PRAME IHC and HLA-A*02:01 up front is the one move that unlocks the whole antigen list, and it is cheap, archival, non-toxic. My only push is that this is a gate, not a therapy, so it should run in parallel with, not ahead of, actually reserving trial slots. The 56% osteosarcoma PRAME positivity (pmid:28315425) means the PRAME axis is likelier than not to survive the test.

Ranking tarlatamab over IMA203 rewards RCT tier but ignores that every tarlatamab efficacy row is SCLC (pmid:40454646) while IMA203's 54% ORR (95% CI 34-73, pmid:38821093) comes from a basket that actually names a sarcoma cohort. On the patient's own PRAME axis the higher-ceiling option also has the closer tumor match, so 'best-validated mechanism' and 'best bet for this patient' point in different directions. A wide CI on n=28 is still the biggest signal in the dossier, and at a 0.85 efficacy weight I take it over an OS curve from a different disease.

target_intervention_label: tarlatamab (DLL3 x CD3 BiTE) via NCT06788938
comment: Holding IMA203 at rank 3 for its one septic death in n=28 (pmid:38821093) is the safety tail dominating a 54% ORR, which inverts the stated efficacy_toxicity_weight of 0.85. The tarlatamab you rank first has zero osteosarcoma data and an entirely SCLC-derived efficacy case (pmid:40454646), so the 'well-characterized' edge is a characterization of the wrong disease. For a patient who put high-risk high-reward on the record, the durable-remission upside of the TCR-T is exactly the trade they signed up for.

target_intervention_label: Confirmatory workup: PRAME IHC + HLA-A*02:01 + DLL3 IHC
comment: Right call to batch all three tests day one and to name the 1-3 week delay as worth it, since skipping the workup forecloses every option the patient asked about. The HLA-A*02:01 coin-flip (~40-50% prevalence) is the real chokepoint, so I would run the typing first-in-line to fail fast on the PRAME half. This is the pick I would put my name next to without qualification.

We land in the same place: IMA203 is the on-axis pick with real numbers, ORR 54% (95% CI 34-73, pmid:38821093), a named sarcoma cohort, and a toxicity profile that matches a 0.85 efficacy weight rather than violating any declared veto (there are none). I would only flag that the sarcoma-cohort activity so far leans on synovial histology, so osteosarcoma-specific response stays a hypothesis until read out. Still the strongest single shot on the board.

This is the pick I most want to push back on. IMA203 sits at rank 1 on a 54% ORR, but the safety tail underneath that number is the heaviest in the dossier: one treatment-related death from septic shock in n=28 (4%), CRS in essentially everyone with G>=3 at 11%, ICANS-like events around 25%, and G>=3 cytopenias in 100% after Cy/Flu. A dead patient in a 28-person series is not a footnote you rank past. The 0.85 efficacy weight is real and I am not disputing that the user accepts risk, but 'accepts high-risk' is not the same as 'ranks the one option with a on-study fatality above two agents that hit the same antigens without killing anyone.' I would not put this first.

Ranking the combination last is the right instinct and I share it. The reason to keep it low is specific: there is no published AE profile for tarlatamab plus RT at all, registry-only, no results tab. Layering concurrent radiation onto a CRS/ICANS-prone BiTE is exactly the kind of synergistic toxicity that a dedicated combination trial has to characterize before anyone can quote a management algorithm for it. The monotherapy basket gives the same backbone with a written step-up-and-tocilizumab protocol behind it, so this stays below rank 2 for me until the RT arm reports.

The rank-1 batched workup is the correct lead and I have no quarrel with it. My problem is IMA203 at rank 2, ahead of both tarlatamab and the ImmTAC. Framing this as 'the profile the patient said they wanted' folds the on-study septic death (1/28), the uniform CRS with G>=3 at 11%, the ~25% ICANS-like rate, and the universal G>=3 post-lymphodepletion cytopenias into a preference the patient never actually named. The user set no toxicity vetoes and asked for high reward; that justifies keeping IMA203 on the list, not slotting it above two same-antigen agents with characterized, managed safety. In a young metastatic patient the immunosuppression window after Cy/Flu is a concrete harm, not an abstraction. I would rank a better-characterized DLL3 or ImmTAC option above it.

Batching the three tests up front is the safest and most information-rich move on the board. It is non-toxic, archival FFPE covers the IHC, one tube covers the HLA typing, and 1-3 weeks buys the confirmation that stops anyone infusing a T-cell engager against a target that may not be on the membrane. No reservation here.

We land in the same place and for the same reason. Tarlatamab is the one agent here with a real safety follow-up: DeLLphi-304 randomized 509 patients, G3+ TRAEs ran 24% on tarlatamab against 53% on chemo, CRS any-grade ~56% but G>=3 ~1%, and the CRS/ICANS has a written step-up-plus-tocilizumab algorithm behind it now. Ranking it first among the enrollable options because the mechanism is best-characterized, not because osteosarcoma benefit is shown, is exactly the discipline I want. The IHC gate carries the weight and we both flag it.

Placing IMA203 below tarlatamab is the ordering I would defend, and your imprecision point (54% off n=28, CI 34-73) does most of the work. I would add the safety half explicitly: the same 28-patient series carries a treatment-related septic death, ~100% CRS with G>=3 ~11%, ~25% ICANS-like events, and universal G>=3 cytopenias after Cy/Flu. So it is not only that the point estimate is soft, it is that the downside is a characterized fatality rather than a theoretical one. The qualifier is only that I would name the toxicity tail alongside the imprecision, not that I disagree with rank 2.

Regorafenib is the safety anchor of this board and I back it at rank 1 on that basis. Two randomized trials in the actual indication (SARC024, REGOBONE), NCCN category 1, and a hand-foot-skin / hypertension / fatigue profile that oncologists have managed for years with dose modification. Modest PFS and no OS signal is a real efficacy ceiling, and the user's high-reward preference is why the antigen-directed trials belong on the list at all, but as the well-characterized fallback with a known AE algorithm this is the correct place to plant it.

Ranking IMA203 above tarlatamab puts an ORR of 54% from n=28 (osteo-prame-ce-2, single-arm ROBINS-I:Moderate, mixed melanoma-heavy basket, one treatment-related septic death) ahead of the one row in this dossier with a randomized OS readout. The 95% CI of 34-73 tells you the point estimate is unstable, and no osteosarcoma patient contributed to it. A named sarcoma cohort on the protocol is an enrollment fact, not efficacy in bone.

Rank 5 (tarlatamab+RT) is osteo-dll3-ce-3, tier 5, registry-only, no results tab and no abstract, and rank 4 (IMC-P115C) has no efficacy readout of its own either. Placing an uncharacterized RT-on-BiTE combination and a first-in-human successor on the ranked list rests on the abscopal hypothesis plus antigen-match, not on data. I would not put a number to either until the phase 1 characterizes the combination toxicity it was built to measure.

Keeping NW-101C on the ranked list because it sits on the patient's PRAME axis borrows its entire efficacy expectation from IMA203; osteo-prame-ce-4 has no publication, no abstract, and the searchable name returns no clinical data. Patient preference is a legitimate tie-breaker, but it cannot promote a tier-5 registry listing into a ranked option. Name it as a fallback slot to verify, not a pick.

The 6-month OS figures cited for the class (94% PRAME-positive vs 40% PRAME-negative) come from osteo-prame-ce-3, an unadjusted subgroup split on an open-label phase-1 melanoma cohort reported as an ASCO 2024 abstract, so I have not seen the full bias profile behind them. That separation is hypothesis-generating and should not carry the weight of a survival claim for a different drug in a different tumor. The workup-first framing at rank 1 is the right call; my objection is only to how the borrowed subset number is deployed.

Ranking tarlatamab first on the strength of its evidence is where I land too: osteo-dll3-ce-2 is DeLLphi-304, RoB2:Low, a pre-specified OS primary that hit (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.47-0.77, p<0.001), replicated in direction by the DeLLphi-301 ORR of 40%. The one caveat to keep load-bearing is that all of it is SCLC (case_match cross_tumor_only) and the DLL3 signal here is RNA, not IHC-confirmed. Best-validated mechanism in the set, osteosarcoma benefit still extrapolated.

The evidence behind regorafenib is not my problem with this pick; SARC024 and REGOBONE are actual randomized osteosarcoma trials, which is more than anything on the DLL3/PRAME axis can show. My qualifier is scope, not quality: the case was nominated around DLL3 and PRAME, and neither regorafenib RCT lives in this dossier's evidence file, so it sits off the axis the board was asked to weigh. Flag the category-1 label too, since ESMO does not formally slot regorafenib and the cross-society convergence is NCCN-weighted.

Cabozantinib rests on CABONE, a single-arm cohort (ORR 11.9%, 6-month non-progression ~33%) with no randomized comparator in osteosarcoma, so calling it a rung below regorafenib is fair but the gap is real: single-arm response rate is a weaker basis than the two RCTs above it. It is still indication-matched osteosarcoma data, which the antigen-directed trials are not. Same scope caveat as regorafenib applies; it is off the nominated DLL3/PRAME axis.

IMA203 carries no consensus category in osteosarcoma; it is guideline-consonant only under the NCCN Bone Cancer v2.2025 clinical-trial recommendation, not as a listed regimen. The ORR 54% is a real signal but comes from an n=28 basket (pmid:38821093), and ranking it first steps over the one option here that is actually category-1, regorafenib on SARC024 and REGOBONE (pmid:31013172, pmid:30477937). If the board wants the biggest number that is a defensible risktaker call, but from the consensus lens it sits well outside the guideline-endorsed population.

target_intervention_label: tarlatamab (DLL3 x CD3 BiTE) via basket NCT06788938
comment: No quarrel with the safety read, and the DLL3 IHC gate the conservative insists on is exactly right. My one qualification is on footing: tarlatamab has no consensus category in bone sarcoma, and DeLLphi-304 (pmid:40454646) is SCLC, so this is a trial-enrollment target under NCCN Bone Cancer v2.2025, not a listed second-line regimen. The guideline-anchored option at that rung is regorafenib, category 1 (pmid:31013172), which the conservative did not rank at all.

The critic ranks tarlatamab first on RCT-grade evidence, and DeLLphi-304 is genuinely the best-validated mechanism in the set (pmid:40454646). But RCT quality in SCLC does not make it guideline-endorsed in osteosarcoma: NCCN Bone Cancer v2.2025 lists no DLL3 agent and slots this only under its clinical-trial recommendation. The category-1 option for this exact relapsed setting, regorafenib on two randomized trials (pmid:31013172, pmid:30477937), is absent from the critic's list, so the strongest evidence-quality pick and the strongest consensus pick are not the same drug here.

Full agreement on ranking the batched DLL3 IHC + PRAME IHC + HLA-A*02:01 workup first. NCCN Bone Cancer v2.2025 makes trial enrollment a preferred pathway for relapsed osteosarcoma, and this is the step that tells you whether any of the on-axis trials are actually open (pmid:35983951, pmid:28315425). Batching the three tests up front is the guideline-consistent move; sequencing them would just delay the same answer.

The advocate dropped regorafenib and cabozantinib from the list, and that is where I part ways: regorafenib is NCCN Bone Cancer v2.2025 category 1 for relapsed osteosarcoma (pmid:31013172, pmid:30477937) and cabozantinib is a listed option (pmid:32078813), so removing them leaves the ranked list with no consensus-endorsed regimen at all. The honest counter is that Libby scopes to the patient's nominated DLL3/PRAME features, and the TKIs are off that targetable-feature axis, so this is a real scope tension rather than a clean error. Still, from the consensus lens the guideline-anchored TKIs should at least be named alongside the antigen-directed trials, not silently cut.

The two RCTs are real and the category-1 label is earned, so this is not an evidence complaint. It is a fit complaint. This patient nominated DLL3 and PRAME, and regorafenib is neither, so it sits outside what Libby was asked to weigh in the first place. On top of that it is a modest-PFS TKI with no OS signal, which is the opposite of what an efficacy weight of 0.85 plus a stated appetite for high-risk high-reward asks for. Fine as a named fallback if the antigen axes both collapse on IHC. Not the lead for a patient who self-selected away from the median.

Same problem as regorafenib and thinner. Off the patient's DLL3/PRAME axis, single-arm CABONE data (ORR ~12%), and even concensusite concedes ESMO does not slot it, so the cross-society backing that carried rank 1 is not here. For a patient carrying a 0.85 efficacy weight and an explicit trial preference, a listed-but-not-converged TKI at rank 2 spends a ranking slot the on-axis baskets have a stronger claim to.

This is the pick I want on record for the patient. Putting the batched DLL3 IHC plus PRAME IHC plus HLA-A*02:01 typing ahead of every drug is what turns prefers_trials from a wish into an actual enrolled slot. The RNA signal cannot open any of these baskets on its own, and a negative HLA type or a negative IHC forecloses a whole axis, so the patient deserves to know that before anyone treats. Non-toxic, archival tissue plus one blood tube, days not months. Ordering it first is not caution overriding the preference, it is the step that protects it.

This is the ranking that reads the patient's stated utility correctly. IMA203 is the biggest efficacy number on the nominated PRAME axis (ORR 54%, mDoR not reached) and the ACTengine basket names a sarcoma cohort outright, so at a 0.85 efficacy weight with an explicit high-risk high-reward appetite this belongs at the top of the drugs. The uniform CRS, ~25% ICANS, lymphodepletion, and the one treatment-related death are real and risktaker surfaces them honestly. With no toxicity veto on file, that profile is one the patient said they would accept for this upside. My only footnote is the gating: this only holds once PRAME IHC and HLA-A*02:01 both confirm.

The evidence caveats are fair and I am not waving them off: n=28, single-arm, wide CI, one treatment-related death, and the responders skew melanoma, not bone. Where I part company is the consequence. Ranking the higher-ORR IMA203 below tarlatamab is an evidence-quality ordering, and for a patient whose weight is 0.85 and who accepts high-risk high-reward, that under-serves the stated efficacy tilt. Tarlatamab has the cleaner phase-3 pedigree, but it is DLL3 and every efficacy row is SCLC, so it is not evidentially safer in this histology, just better-studied in a different one. IMA203 at least names a sarcoma cohort. I would rank the two closer together and let the double biomarker gate, not the SCLC-versus-sarcoma evidence base, decide which one the patient can actually enter.

The toxicity accounting is honest and the numbers are not in dispute: CRS ~100%, G3+ ~11%, ICANS ~25%, universal post-lymphodepletion cytopenias, one septic death in 28. What I am disputing is the weight. Ranking IMA203 third, behind tarlatamab and brenetafusp, is a tolerability-first ordering, and this patient's 0.85 efficacy weight with an explicit high-risk high-reward appetite and no toxicity veto tilts the other way. Conservative names its own prior in the notes, which I respect, but the patient's prior is the one that should set the rank. On the best-tolerated PRAME agent going above the best-responding one, I would flip the priority given what this patient asked for, while keeping every toxicity line conservative wrote in the informed-consent conversation.
